narrative:
The model estimates there’s a 23% chance you won’t pass your final year, which is above the 10% threshold that requires extra support. Because of this, you’ll need to take remedial courses to help you stay on track.

The main reasons the model is concerned come down to three key areas. First, you’ve never failed a class before, which actually works in your favor—it shows you have a solid foundation. However, the model is most worried about how much time you’re spending on your studies. Right now, you’re studying less than two hours a week, while most students who pass dedicate at least two to five hours. This is the biggest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The third important point is your ambition: you’ve said you want to go to university, which the model sees as a positive sign that you’re motivated to succeed.

Other details about your situation also played a role, though less strongly. For example, your parents’ education levels are lower than average among students who pass, and you’re in a romantic relationship, which some research suggests can sometimes reduce study time. On the other hand, you have internet access at home and attended nursery school, both of which are linked to better outcomes.

The good news is that small changes can make a big difference. Increasing your study time—even by a few hours a week—could significantly improve your chances. The remedial courses will give you structured support, and since you’re aiming for higher education, you already have the drive to make it work. Focus on building consistent study habits, and you’ll be in a much stronger position to pass.
